To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the adsorption of Abf2 to stretched DNA is a cooperative process, the adsorption rate is tension dependent and decreases with increasing compaction and that the binding constant is significantly smaller than the value calculated by Brewer et. al. (Biophysical Journal 85 (2004) 2519).

the compaction of DNA in a double flow chamber can be described by a McGhee-von-Hippel model, and that Abf2p has an adsorption constant K=2.5 x 10 (6) M(- 1) for a tension of 1 pN and an adsorption constant that is 2 to 3 orders of magnitude smaller at a tension of 10 pN. In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Abf2p binds to the ends of the stretched DNA, but that the binding constant decreases significantly with increasing DNA compaction.
the compaction of DNA by Abf2p is a cooperative process that depends on the degree of compaction, and that the binding constant decreases with increasing compaction.

the data of Brewer et al. are consistent with a compaction of DNA by Abf2p, but that a more detailed and quantitative analysis of the data is required to obtain reliable values for the adsorption constant K and the foot print of the Abf2p protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Abf2p binds to DNA in a cooperative manner with an average binding constant K=2 x 10(4)M(-1).

the data of Brewer et al. are compatible with the hypothesis that Abf2p is a condensing protein, but the data are also compatible with the hypothesis of a non-compactable protein that binds with a decreasing binding constant to compacting DNA.
the data are consistent with an Abf2p-induced compaction of DNA by a factor of two.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a Langmuir model for the adsorption is not appropriate, and that the binding constant is not constant during compaction.
the binding constant of a protein to dsDNA depends on the degree of DNA compaction.
Abf2p is an efficient compactor of dsDNA in vitro, but that the binding constant decreases by a factor of at least 10 as DNA becomes more compact.
